source_title: Charles Schulz Believed This Charlie Brown Special Was His Real Masterpiece
source_excerpt:
Renan is the Anime Lead Editor for GameRant. Ren graduated Cum Laude from Lesley University in 2017 and has been focusing exclusively on his journalistic endeavors ever since. When Ren isn't working, he's usually playing video games or reading.
From Charlie Brown's annual Christmas struggles to Linus' seemingly endless search for the Great Pumpkin, Charles Schulz's Peanuts is responsible for some of the most beloved holiday traditions in television history. Even though A Charlie Brown Christmas usually gets the most love and attention, there's an argument to be made that It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown is actually Schulz's best work – and he'd be inclined to agree.
Originally airing in 1966, Charlie Brown's bleak trick-or-treating experience and Snoopy's World War I adventure made the special an immediate success. The influence of It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown has extended far beyond ever since. Between its beautiful animation, immersive atmosphere, and surprisingly thoughtful exploration of childhood faith, there's a good reason the Great Pumpkin is still one of the most recognizable parts of The Peanuts ' legacy.
It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown Was a Major Achievement for Charles Schulz
Following the enormous success of A Charlie Brown Christmas in 1965, CBS wanted another animated special that could capture the same magic. Charles Schulz ended up reuniting with producer Lee Mendelson and animator Bill Melendez to develop a Halloween story, this time drawing inspiration from the Great Pumpkin storyline he'd been writing in his Peanuts comic strip. The resulting 25-minute special premiered on October 27, 1966, and proved just how much creative potential Schulz's relatively simple comic strip characters had on television.
Linus' unwavering belief in the Great Pumpkin revealed a more innocent side of his character. In a 1979 interview, Schulz reflected on It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown , saying, "Linus and the pumpkin patch came to me as an idea one year when I was trying to imagine what would happen if a child suddenly got one holiday ahead of himself and began to wait for presents on Halloween rather than Christmas. Then, of course, he had to wait for someone to bring him these presents. And who would it be on Halloween night other than – obviously – the Great Pumpkin. I really am very proud of this whole idea, and it may be the most original – or unique – of all my ideas during these past thirty years.”⁠ Given the special's legacy, it's hard not to agree with Schulz.
The Peanuts Comics Kept the Great Pumpkin Alive for Decades
Although It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown introduced millions to Linus' unusual Halloween tradition, Schulz had already been working on the storyline for years at that point. The Great Pumpkin debuted in The Peanuts in October 1959, when Linus explained that children should write letters to the mysterious holiday figure requesting Halloween presents. Much like Santa Claus, the Great Pumpkin rewarded good children, except that he emerged from the most sincere pumpkin patch rather than arriving in a sleigh.
Naturally, Charlie Brown and the other members of the Peanuts gang were considerably less enthusiastic about Linus' theory. Their skepticism became an important part of the storyline, especially as Linus kept waiting for something that never came. Schulz would regularly go back to the Great Pumpkin during the strip's run, turning Linus' annual vigil into one of The Peanuts ' most iconic traditions.
It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown is a Halloween Institution
Few animated television specials have maintained the cultural relevance of It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown . It was a major success at release, earning two Emmy nominations in 1967, including one for Outstanding Children's Program. The special quickly became an essential Halloween television, introducing new generations to Charlie Brown, Linus, Snoopy, and the world Schulz created. Even people who haven't watched the special are familiar with moments like Charlie Brown getting a rock.
The special's legacy has endured even as the way audiences watch holiday television has changed. After decades of network broadcasts, the classic Peanuts specials moved to Apple TV+ in 2020. The move away from traditional television prompted some disappointment among longtime viewers, but it hasn't taken away the special's importance to the franchise. In fact, Apple TV+ makes It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown free every year to capture the feeling of watching it on television as it aired for real.
